instructors.name: Maya Okafor
instructors.bio: Maya has photographed weddings, markets and mountain mornings for fourteen years. She teaches the few habits that make the biggest difference to a picture: where the light comes from, what stays in the frame and when to press the button.

instructors.name: Luis Herrera
instructors.bio: Luis builds the reports that other people rely on. He teaches spreadsheets the way he wishes he had learned them: start with a question, keep the data tidy and let formulas do the repeating.

instructors.name: Priya Raman
instructors.bio: Priya cooks for a busy family and writes recipes that work on a Tuesday night. Her courses are about technique first, so one skill opens many dishes.

instructors.name: Tomasz Wren
instructors.bio: Tomasz draws every day and keeps a sketchbook for each year. He teaches drawing as a way of seeing, with small exercises that fit into a coffee break.

courses.title: Light and Composition
courses.summary: Learn to see light and frame a picture. No special camera needed.
courses.description: A friendly first course in photography. You will learn how light shapes a picture, how to arrange what is in the frame and how to take the same scene three ways so you can choose the best one. Everything is taught with the camera you already own, including a phone.
courses.outcomes:
Read the direction and softness of light
Use the rule of thirds, lines and framing on purpose
Set exposure so your pictures are not too dark or too bright
Build a small set of pictures you are proud of

lessons.title: Why some pictures work
lessons.notes:
A good picture is rarely about the camera. It is about where the light falls, what you chose to leave out and the moment you pressed the button.
Take a walk and look at ordinary things for ten minutes before you take a single picture.
lessons.summary: Look at four pictures and say why one is better.

lessons.title: Reading the light
lessons.notes:
Light from the side shows shape. Light from behind makes a glow. Light from above flattens a face.
Note the time and the weather next to every picture you take this week.
lessons.summary: Direction, softness and colour of light through the day.

lessons.title: Framing and the rule of thirds
lessons.notes:
Imagine a grid of nine boxes. Put the thing you care about on a crossing line and give it room to look into.
Try the same subject centred, then off to one side, and compare.
lessons.summary: Place your subject and use lines to lead the eye.

lessons.title: Exposure without the maths
lessons.notes:
Three things control brightness: how long the shutter is open, how wide the hole is and how sensitive the sensor is.
On a phone, tap the screen where the subject is and slide the brightness until it looks right.
lessons.summary: Brightness, shutter and aperture in plain words.

lessons.title: Shoot one scene three ways
lessons.notes:
Pick one scene near your home. Shoot it wide, then close, then from low down.
Sort your pictures and write one line about why you chose your favourite.
lessons.summary: A practical exercise to put it all together.

lessons.title: Choosing and sharing your best
lessons.notes:
Crop to improve the frame, nudge the brightness and stop there.
Show three pictures, not thirty.
lessons.summary: Edit lightly and pick the pictures worth showing.

courses.title: Portraits by Window Light
courses.summary: Make warm, natural portraits at home with one window and a sheet of card.
courses.description: Window light is the softest, kindest light there is. In this course you will place a person, a window and a simple reflector to make portraits with depth and a natural look, without buying lights.
courses.outcomes:
Position a subject to a window for flattering light
Use a reflector made from card or a sheet
Direct a relaxed person and choose the moment
Edit portraits so skin looks natural

lessons.title: The window as a studio
lessons.notes:
North-facing windows give steady light, while a sunny window gives strong contrast. Hang a thin white curtain to soften harsh sun.
Stand at the window and look at how the light falls on your own hand.
lessons.summary: Find the best window in your home and test it.

lessons.title: Placing your subject
lessons.notes:
Turn the face slightly toward the window until a small triangle of light appears on the shadow-side cheek.
Move the person a step at a time and watch the catch-lights in the eyes.
lessons.summary: Angles between the face, the window and the camera.

lessons.title: Fill with a reflector
lessons.notes:
Hold a sheet of white card opposite the window to bounce soft light back into the shadow side.
Move it closer for more fill and farther for less.
lessons.summary: Lift the shadows with white card.

lessons.title: Directing a relaxed person
lessons.notes:
People relax when they have something to do. Ask a question and shoot while they answer.
Keep your camera up and keep talking.
lessons.summary: Talk, pause and wait for the real expression.

lessons.title: Editing for natural skin
lessons.notes:
Fix brightness and colour first. Soften only what distracts.
Compare with the original often so you do not drift too far.
lessons.summary: Simple, honest retouching.

courses.title: Spreadsheets From Scratch
courses.summary: Build your first useful spreadsheet and understand every cell.
courses.description: You will start with an empty grid and finish with a working household budget. Along the way you will learn how cells, rows and formulas behave, how to keep data tidy and how to make a simple chart that people understand at a glance.
courses.outcomes:
Enter, format and sort data with confidence
Write sums, averages and simple IF formulas
Use absolute and relative references correctly
Make a clear chart and a printable budget

lessons.title: The grid and your first numbers
lessons.notes:
A spreadsheet is a table where every cell has an address such as B3. Type a number, press Enter and you have started.
Practise with the arrow keys and Tab until you do not need the mouse.
lessons.summary: Cells, rows, columns and moving around quickly.

lessons.title: Formulas: sums and averages
lessons.notes:
A formula always starts with an equals sign. =SUM(B2:B8) adds a range and =AVERAGE(B2:B8) finds the middle.
Change a number and watch the total update by itself.
lessons.summary: Let the sheet do the arithmetic.

lessons.title: Keeping data tidy
lessons.notes:
Put headings in the top row and keep blank rows out of the middle of your data.
Tidy data can be sorted, filtered and charted with no extra work.
lessons.summary: One fact per cell, one row per thing.

lessons.title: Copying formulas: references
lessons.notes:
When you drag a formula down, cell addresses move with it. A dollar sign, as in $B$1, pins a reference in place.
Use a pinned cell for a tax rate or a monthly limit.
lessons.summary: Relative and absolute references, with a dollar sign.

lessons.title: Making decisions with IF
lessons.notes:
=IF(B2>100,"Over","OK") checks the number and returns one of two answers.
Add conditional colours so the sheet shows problems for you.
lessons.summary: Show a message or a number depending on a test.

lessons.title: A chart people understand
lessons.notes:
Use a bar chart to compare, a line chart for change over time and avoid 3D effects.
Give the chart a title that says what it shows.
lessons.summary: Pick the right chart and remove the clutter.

courses.title: Pivot Tables and Dashboards
courses.summary: Summarise thousands of rows in seconds and present them on one page.
courses.description: For people who already know formulas. You will turn a long list of sales into pivot tables, slice them live and assemble a one-page dashboard that updates when new data arrives.
courses.outcomes:
Build pivot tables from a clean table
Group by date, category and region
Use lookups to join two lists
Publish a dashboard with slicers

lessons.title: From a list to a table
lessons.notes:
Convert the range to a table so new rows are picked up automatically.
Check for blank cells, text numbers and duplicate headings.
lessons.summary: Prepare data so a pivot table can use it.

lessons.title: Your first pivot table
lessons.notes:
Drag a field to Rows, another to Values and see the summary appear.
Try the same fields in a different place and notice what changes.
lessons.summary: Rows, columns, values and filters.

lessons.title: Grouping dates and numbers
lessons.notes:
Group a date field by month to see the shape of the year.
Group ages or prices into bands to find patterns.
lessons.summary: Months, quarters and bands.

lessons.title: Lookups that join lists
lessons.notes:
Use XLOOKUP, or INDEX with MATCH, to fetch a value by its code.
Wrap the formula in IFERROR so missing codes do not break the sheet.
lessons.summary: Bring a price or a name from another sheet.

lessons.title: Slicers and charts
lessons.notes:
A slicer is a set of buttons that filters one or many pivots at once.
Link a chart to the pivot so it changes with the slicer.
lessons.summary: Make the pivot interactive.

lessons.title: Assemble the dashboard
lessons.notes:
Decide the question first. Put the most important number top left.
Leave space around each chart and use one colour for one meaning.
lessons.summary: One page, four numbers and two charts.

courses.title: Weeknight Cooking Basics
courses.summary: Five techniques that make a quick, good dinner from almost anything.
courses.description: Cooking is easier when you know a few techniques well. We cover knife work, heat, seasoning, a one-pan dinner and a sauce that rescues leftovers, using a small shelf of ingredients that keep well.
courses.outcomes:
Cut vegetables quickly and safely
Control heat so food browns and does not burn
Season in layers and taste as you go
Cook a full dinner in one pan in thirty minutes

lessons.title: Your kitchen kit and your knife
lessons.notes:
One good knife, a board, a pan and a pot will take you a long way.
Curl the fingers of your guiding hand and let the knife glide against your knuckles.
lessons.summary: What you need, and how to hold a knife.

lessons.title: Heat and browning
lessons.notes:
Pat food dry and let the pan get hot before the food goes in.
Leave it alone until it lets go of the pan by itself.
lessons.summary: Why a hot dry pan matters.

lessons.title: Seasoning and tasting
lessons.notes:
Salt in small amounts at each stage, then finish with lemon or vinegar.
Taste, adjust and taste again.
lessons.summary: Salt, acid and fat in the right order.

lessons.title: One-pan chicken and vegetables
lessons.notes:
Start with the pieces that take longest and add the quick ones later.
A meat thermometer saves guessing.
lessons.summary: A whole dinner, one dish to wash.

lessons.title: The pan sauce and leftovers
lessons.notes:
Pour in a splash of stock, scrape the pan and let it bubble until it coats a spoon.
Stir in a small knob of butter at the end.
lessons.summary: Turn the browned bits into a sauce.

courses.title: Bread and Baking at Home
courses.summary: Bake a loaf you are proud of, then use the same dough for rolls and flatbreads.
courses.description: Bread is flour, water, salt and time. You will learn why dough behaves as it does, how to shape and score a loaf and how to fix the common problems, using only a bowl, an oven and a heavy pot.
courses.outcomes:
Mix and knead or fold a simple dough
Judge when dough has risen enough
Shape, score and bake with steam
Troubleshoot dense or flat loaves

lessons.title: What flour, water and yeast do
lessons.notes:
Water wakes the flour, kneading builds structure and yeast makes the gas that lifts it.
Weigh your ingredients for the same loaf each time.
lessons.summary: The science in a few minutes.

lessons.title: Mixing and folding
lessons.notes:
Rest the dough and fold it a few times instead of long kneading.
Wet your hands so the dough does not stick.
lessons.summary: No-knead and kneaded doughs.

lessons.title: Rising and the poke test
lessons.notes:
Press a floured finger in. If the dent springs back slowly, it is ready.
A cooler room means a slower and tastier rise.
lessons.summary: Know when it is ready.

lessons.title: Shaping and scoring
lessons.notes:
Pull the dough toward you to tighten the skin.
Score with a sharp blade at a shallow angle so the loaf can open.
lessons.summary: Tension on the surface gives a good shape.

lessons.title: Baking with steam
lessons.notes:
Preheat the pot, drop in the dough and bake with the lid on for the first half.
Cool the loaf fully before you slice it.
lessons.summary: A heavy pot makes a bakery crust.

lessons.title: Fixing problems and using the dough
lessons.notes:
Most bread problems are timing problems. Write down the time and temperature each bake.
Roll the same dough thin for flatbreads.
lessons.summary: Dense, flat, pale and what to do next.

courses.title: Drawing Foundations
courses.summary: Learn to see shapes, lines and light, and draw what is in front of you.
courses.description: No talent required. You will practise a handful of exercises that train your eye: contour lines, basic shapes, proportion, light and shadow. By the end you will draw a small still life from observation.
courses.outcomes:
Draw confident lines instead of timid ones
Break objects into simple shapes
Measure proportions by eye
Shade a form so it looks solid

lessons.title: Warm up: lines and circles
lessons.notes:
Draw from the shoulder, not the wrist. Fill a page with long lines and loops.
Do this warm-up before every session.
lessons.summary: Loosen your hand with a few simple marks.

lessons.title: Seeing shapes
lessons.notes:
Everything is a mix of boxes, cylinders and spheres.
Sketch the big shape first and add detail last.
lessons.summary: Break a cup, a pear and a book into basic forms.

lessons.title: Contour and blind contour
lessons.notes:
Draw the edge of an object without looking at the paper.
The drawings look odd and train your eye very quickly.
lessons.summary: Slow, careful looking.

lessons.title: Proportion and measuring
lessons.notes:
Hold the pencil at arm's length and compare one height with another.
Check the angles by holding the pencil against them.
lessons.summary: Use a pencil as a ruler.

lessons.title: Light, shadow and form
lessons.notes:
Find the lightest light, the darkest dark and the soft edge between them.
Build shade with light layers, not one heavy press.
lessons.summary: Shade a sphere and a cup.

lessons.title: A still life from start to finish
lessons.notes:
Arrange three objects by a lamp. Place them lightly, measure and shade.
Step away from the drawing often.
lessons.summary: Put every skill into one drawing.

courses.title: Figure Sketching in Ink
courses.summary: Capture a person in a few confident lines, with pen and brush.
courses.description: A course for people who already draw. You will sketch gesture in under a minute, build a figure from simple forms and use ink lines and washes to suggest weight, cloth and light.
courses.outcomes:
Capture gesture in 30 to 60 seconds
Build a figure from simple volumes
Use line weight and a brush wash
Finish a sheet of figure studies

lessons.title: Gesture in one minute
lessons.notes:
Draw one flowing line through the spine and limbs.
Set a timer and do ten sketches in ten minutes.
lessons.summary: Catch the action before the details.

lessons.title: Building with simple forms
lessons.notes:
Think of the torso as two boxes that can tilt against each other.
Draw through the form so the pose looks solid.
lessons.summary: Ribcage, pelvis and limbs as volumes.

lessons.title: Line weight and confidence
lessons.notes:
Press harder where the form turns away or sits in shadow.
Let one line say a lot.
lessons.summary: Heavier lines near the viewer and in shadow.

lessons.title: Cloth and folds
lessons.notes:
Look for the point where the cloth is held and the folds spread from it.
Draw fewer folds, with clear purpose.
lessons.summary: Folds follow tension and gravity.

lessons.title: Brush wash and tone
lessons.notes:
Dilute ink with water and lay one flat wash for shadow.
Let the wash dry before a second layer.
lessons.summary: Add depth with thin ink.

lessons.title: A sheet of figure studies
lessons.notes:
Fill a page with eight poses of different lengths.
Choose your favourite and write down what worked.
lessons.summary: Combine everything in a full page.

questions.text: Which light shows the shape of a face best?
questions.why: Side light creates gentle shadows that show shape.

questions.text: What does soft light usually come from?
options: A large, diffused source such as an overcast sky
questions.why: A large source wraps around the subject.

questions.text: In the rule of thirds, where do you place the subject?
options: On a crossing line of a nine-box grid

questions.text: Your picture looks too dark. What can you do first?
options: Move the brightness up or expose for the subject

questions.text: Why shoot one scene three ways?
options: To compare and choose the best framing

questions.text: How many pictures should you share from a set?
questions.why: Editing is part of the craft.

questions.text: How do you soften harsh sun at a window?
questions.why: A sheer curtain diffuses the sun.

questions.text: What does a reflector do?
options: Changes the colour of the walls

questions.text: A relaxed expression comes most easily when you...
options: Ask the person to hold still
Keep them talking while you shoot

questions.text: In editing portraits, what should you fix first?
Every formula begins with...
questions.why: The equals sign tells the sheet to calculate.

questions.text: What does =SUM(B2:B8) do?
options: Adds the cells from B2 to B8

questions.text: What does a dollar sign in $B$1 do?
questions.why: An absolute reference does not move.

questions.text: Which chart is best for change over time?
What is tidy data?
options: One fact per cell and one row per thing
Colours that mean something to you
questions.why: Tidy data works with every tool.

questions.text: =IF(B2>100,"Over","OK") returns...
options: Over when B2 is larger than 100
questions.why: IF returns one of two answers.

questions.text: A pivot table works best when the source is...
What does a slicer do?
questions.why: It filters one or many pivots.

questions.text: Which formula fetches a price by code?
Where does the most important number go on a dashboard?
questions.why: Readers start at the top left.

questions.text: Why pat meat dry before searing?
options: So it browns instead of steaming

questions.text: When should you season?
options: In layers, tasting as you go

questions.text: What helps a pan sauce thicken?
How do you hold food while cutting?
What makes dough rise?
How do you know dough has risen enough?
options: A floured finger leaves a dent that springs back slowly

questions.text: Why bake in a covered heavy pot?
options: It traps steam for a better crust
questions.why: Steam keeps the surface soft so the loaf expands.

questions.text: A dense loaf is often a problem of...
Where should the warm-up marks come from?
questions.why: Shoulder strokes are smoother and bolder.

questions.text: What is blind contour for?
options: Training your eye to look slowly

questions.text: How can a pencil help measure?
options: Held at arm's length as a ruler
As a pointer to the paper

questions.text: How do you build smooth shading?
What is a gesture drawing?
options: A quick drawing of the movement of a pose

questions.text: Where do you press harder with the pen?
options: Where the form turns away or in shadow

questions.text: Cloth folds spread from...
A wash should dry before...

items.title: How do the courses work?
items.text: Each course is a list of short video lessons with notes. Mark a lesson complete when you finish it, pass the quizzes and your certificate is issued when everything is done.

items.title: Can I try a course before paying?
items.text: Yes. The first lesson of every course is a free preview. You can watch it without an account.

items.title: How do I pay?
items.text: By card, through Stripe Checkout. As soon as the payment is confirmed the course opens in My courses.

items.title: What is the refund policy?
items.text: You can ask for a refund from My account. The conditions (how many days, how much progress, and that no certificate has been issued) are on the Terms and refunds page. Every request is checked by a person, also those outside the conditions.

items.title: What happens if I get a full refund?
items.text: Your access ends. Your progress is kept but locked, and a certificate you were given is revoked. You can enrol again at any time by paying again.

items.title: How long do I have access?
items.text: For as long as your enrolment is active. There is no expiry date.

items.title: How do certificates work?
items.text: When you have completed every lesson and passed every quiz, a printable certificate with a check code appears. Anyone can check the code on the Certificate page.

items.title: Can I watch on my phone?
items.text: Yes. The site works on phones, tablets and computers, and your progress is the same everywhere.

items.title: I forgot my password.
items.text: Write to us from the Contact page with the email you used and we will help.

We keep the catalog small on purpose, so every course gets the care it needs.

blocks.title: Terms and refunds
blocks.text:
These terms are short on purpose. By paying for a course you agree to them.

  • One payment gives you the course for as long as your enrolment is active.
  • Courses are for your own use. Please do not share your account.
  • We may update lessons to keep them correct.

blocks.title: Refund conditions
blocks.text: You can ask for a refund from My account. A person at {name} checks every request.

blocks.title: How a refund request is handled
blocks.text:
A request inside the conditions is marked eligible. A request outside them can still be sent and is marked outside policy; we look at it case by case.

If we approve a full refund, your access ends, your progress is kept but locked, and any certificate you were given is revoked. You can enrol again by paying again.

A partial goodwill refund returns part of the price and your access stays. If we decline, we tell you why.

blocks.title: Say hello
blocks.text: Questions about a course, an order or a refund? Send us a note and we will reply by email.

blocks.title: Verify a certificate
blocks.text: Type the code printed on a certificate, for example BPA-XXXX-XXXX, to check that it is real.

blocks.title: What a certificate means
blocks.text: A certificate is issued only when a student has completed every lesson and passed every quiz in a course. If a student is refunded in full, the certificate is revoked and this page says so.
